title: Concurrency probe for batching amplification and queueing effects across heterogeneous request mixes
creator: Jordan Kim
description:
Goal: quantify how increasing concurrency in a multi-class traffic mix amplifies continuous-batching inefficiencies and queueing-induced tail latency. We need a repeatable probe that measures tokens/sec, p95/p99 request latency, token-level service time, queue length distribution, and the point where batching no longer improves unit cost due to queue growth. The output will drive runtime scheduling recommendations and autoscaler guardrails.

Scope & what this ticket delivers:
- A parametrized load probe (concurrency sweep + arrival pattern generator) that can simulate 3 workload classes simultaneously: short-chat (avg 30 tokens), long-completion (avg 1200 tokens), and embedding requests (payload-oriented).
- Traffic profiles: Poisson baseline, bursty (Weibull inter-arrival), and steady high-concurrency tail probes.
- KV-cache hit toggles (0%, 60%, 90%) and session affinity layers to recreate warm vs cold sequences.
- Metrics captured: tokens_per_sec (aggregate + per-class), p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (generation-only and end-to-end), queue length histogram, average batch size, batching wait-time distribution, and throughput-per-GPU.
- Regression detection: automated comparison to baseline runs using effect size (Cohen's d) and sequential probability ratio tests; we set an alert when p95 increases by >15% AND tokens/sec drops by >8% for two consecutive cycles.
- Deliverables: Jupyter analysis notebooks, Grafana dashboard panels, a benchmark-run artifact for CI, and a short Confluence doc with recommended runtime knob adjustments (batch window, max-batch, preemptive dequeue thresholds).

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Concurrency sweep: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 active users per shard.
- Workload mix ratios to test: 70/20/10 (chat/long/embeddings), 30/60/10, 50/30/20 (to stress long completions).
- Arrival pattern: poisson / bursty-90th / periodic micro-bursts (5s spikes).
- Cache hit: cold / warm (60%) / hot (90%).
- Batch policy variants: immediate/continuous-window(5ms,10ms,20ms)/max-batch caps (32,64,128).

Success criteria:
- Reproducible plots showing at what concurrency x the average batch size increases but tokens/sec per GPU plateaus or declines.
- Detectable inflection point where p95 jumps >20ms relative to baseline.
- A reproducible threshold recommendation for when the autoscaler should scale out aggressively instead of relying on longer batch windows.
- CI artifact + smoke test that runs a short sweep and fails if p95 regresses by the alerting rule above.

Implementation notes & trade-offs:
- We will run the initial sweep against a single GPU profile (A100-40GB equivalent) to isolate controller behavior; follow-ups will repeat on mixed hardware.
- To avoid masking queue dynamics, the generator must not retry failed requests; instead it should record them and surface retry patterns.
- Capturing token-level service time requires instrumenting the serving runtime to annotate per-request token emission timestamps; minimal patch will emit structured logs to the existing tracing pipeline (tempo -> logs -> S3) for offline analysis.
- We trade off experiment run time for statistical power: longer runs reduce noise but slow iteration. Start with 10-minute steady windows per sweep point, extend to 30 minutes for points near the observed inflection.

Notes on metrics definitions (important for consistency):
- tokens_per_sec: sum(tokens_emitted)/wall_clock_window per GPU and normalized per active session.
- batch_wait_time: time between first request in batch and batch dispatch. exclude tiny micro-batches (<2 requests) from median calculations but keep them for tail analysis.
- p95: measured on end-to-end request completion including serialization and any post-processing hooks.
